summary: Describes Oblivious DNS over HTTPS, a protocol where a proxy relays encrypted DoH messages so a client's IP address is hidden from the DNS resolver. No single server sees both who asked and what was asked. It was developed outside the IETF and published for interoperability and experimentation. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: When a resolver looks up a name for you, it learns your address and the name at the same time. This RFC splits the lookup in two: one server carries the question and another reads it, so that neither of them can tell who asked. The client encrypts the question for the resolver, and the proxy that carries it cannot open it.

questions: how to hide ip from dns resolver
what is oblivious dns over https
how does oblivious doh hide the client ip address
subtitle: Splitting a DNS query across two servers so neither one knows both who asked and what was asked.

tldr.problem: DNS over HTTPS hides the contents of a query from eavesdroppers, but the resolver still learns the client's IP address, and so learns who is asking and roughly where from.
tldr.mechanism: The client encrypts the query with the target's public key, sends it to a proxy, and the proxy forwards it to the target; the target answers and encrypts the reply with a key derived from the original request, so the proxy learns neither the query nor the answer.
tldr.outcome: As long as the proxy and the target do not collude, no single server holds both the client's address and the query. The protocol is Experimental and carries one new media type.

today: RFC 9230 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document describes a long-running experiment to assess deployment viability and measure resolution latency, and says implementations not involved in the experiment will not recognize the protocol.

sections.title: Hiding the Client from the Resolver
sections.content:
DNS over HTTPS (DoH), RFC 8484, defines a mechanism to allow DNS messages to be transmitted in HTTP messages protected with TLS. This provides improved confidentiality and authentication for DNS interactions in various circumstances.

While DoH can prevent eavesdroppers from directly reading the contents of DNS exchanges, clients cannot send DNS queries to and receive answers from servers without revealing their local IP address, and thus information about the identity or location of the client, to the server.

Proposals such as Oblivious DNS increase privacy by ensuring that no single DNS server is aware of both the client IP address and the message contents. This document defines Oblivious DoH, an experimental protocol built on DoH that permits proxied resolution, in which DNS messages are encrypted so that no server can independently read both the client IP address and the DNS message contents.

As with DoH, DNS messages exchanged over Oblivious DoH are fully formed DNS messages. Clients that want answers that are relevant to the network they are on without revealing their exact IP address can thus use the EDNS0 Client Subnet option (RFC 7871, Section 7.1.2) to provide a hint to the resolver.

The protocol was developed outside the IETF and is published here to guide implementation, ensure interoperability among implementations and enable wide-scale experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a resolver looks up a name for you, it learns your address and the name at the same time. This RFC splits the lookup in two: one server carries the question and another reads it, so that neither of them can tell who asked. The client encrypts the question for the resolver, and the proxy that carries it cannot open it.

sections.title: The Three-Party Exchange
sections.content:
Oblivious hostname resolution over DoH involves three parties. The Client generates queries and is responsible for selecting the combination of proxy and target to use for a given query. The Proxy is an HTTP server that proxies encrypted DNS queries and responses between the client and the target, and is identified by a URI Template (RFC 6570). It is not acting as a full HTTP proxy, but is a specialized server used to forward Oblivious DNS messages. The Target is an HTTP server that receives and decrypts encrypted client queries from a proxy and returns encrypted responses via that same proxy. To provide DNS responses the target can be a DNS resolver, be co-located with a resolver, or forward to a resolver.

Queries are created by the client and sent to the proxy as HTTP requests using the POST method. Clients are configured with a proxy URI Template and the target URI, and the scheme for both MUST be https. The proxy URI Template uses the Level 3 encoding of RFC 6570 and contains two variables, targethost for the hostname of the target server and targetpath for the path on which the target is accessible. The template MUST contain both variables exactly once and MUST NOT contain any other variables, and the variables MUST be within the path or query components of the URI. Clients MUST ignore configurations that do not conform to this template.

Oblivious DoH messages have no cache value, since both requests and responses are encrypted using ephemeral key material, so requests and responses MUST NOT be cached. Clients MUST set the HTTP Content-Type header to application/oblivious-dns-message, and SHOULD set the same value for the Accept header. If the proxy fails to match the targethost and targetpath variables it MUST treat the request as malformed and return a 4xx client error with a Proxy-Status response header carrying an error parameter of type http_request_error. If the proxy cannot establish a connection to the target it can indicate this with a 502 status code, and it may refuse to forward connections to non-standard ports with a 403 and an error type of http_request_denied.

The response is generated by the target and MUST set the Content-Type header to application/oblivious-dns-message, and the proxy MUST use the same type on all successful responses it sends to the client. A client MUST only consider a response that contains the Content-Type header before processing the payload, and a response without it MUST be treated as an error. Proxies forward responses from the target to the client without any modification to the body or status code, and SHOULD add a Proxy-Status response header with a received-status parameter indicating that the status code came from the target. If a client receives a 3xx status code and follows a redirect, the subsequent request MUST also be performed through a proxy. A DNS response indicating failure, such as SERVFAIL or NXDOMAIN, still uses a successful 2xx HTTP status code as long as the DNS response is valid.

Metadata sent with these messages could weaken or remove the privacy properties, so proxies MUST NOT send any client-identifying information to targets, such as Forwarded HTTP headers, and clients MUST NOT include private state in requests to proxies, such as HTTP cookies.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties take part. The client picks a proxy and a target, and sends the proxy a normal HTTPS POST whose body is the encrypted question. The proxy reads the target's name and path out of the request URL and forwards the same body to it. The target decrypts, looks up the name, encrypts the answer and sends it back through the proxy to the client.

sections.title: The ObliviousDoHMessage Format
sections.content:
There are two types of Oblivious DoH message: queries, with message type 0x01, and responses, with message type 0x02. Both carry a DNS message, which is either a query or a response depending on context, and padding of arbitrary length, which MUST contain all zeros. They are encoded as a structure with an opaque dns_message field of 1 to 2^16-1 bytes and an opaque padding field of 0 to 2^16-1 bytes.

An encrypted plaintext is carried in an ObliviousDoHMessage, which has a one-byte message_type, an opaque key_id field of 0 to 2^16-1 bytes, and an opaque encrypted_message field of 1 to 2^16-1 bytes. Implementations MAY enforce limits on the size of the encrypted field, depending on the size of plaintext DNS messages; DNS queries, for example, will not reach the size limit of 2^16-1 in practice.

The key_id is the identifier of the corresponding configuration key, computed as Expand(Extract("", config), "odoh key id", Nh), where config is the configuration contents structure and Extract, Expand and Nh are as specified by the HPKE cipher suite key derivation function. For a query, the encrypted message holds the encrypted query for the target. For a response, the key_id field carries a fresh random nonce instead, so that the client can derive the same secrets.

The configuration itself is encoded with TLS-style encoding. An ObliviousDoHConfigContents structure holds a key encapsulation mechanism identifier, a key derivation function identifier, an authenticated encryption with associated data identifier, and an opaque public key. An ObliviousDoHConfig structure holds a version and a length, and a list of configurations contains one or more of them in decreasing order of preference, so that a server can support multiple versions and parameter sets. Clients MUST ignore any configuration structure with a version they do not support, and also with a KEM, KDF or AEAD they do not support. The version of Oblivious DoH specified in this document is 0x0001.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a one-byte type, a variable-length key identifier, and the encrypted payload. The plain payload is the DNS message followed by padding, and the padding must be all zero bytes so that the receiver can check it was not tampered with.

sections.title: Encryption with HPKE
sections.content:
Oblivious DoH uses Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) for public key encryption. In the absence of an application profile standard specifying otherwise, a compliant implementation MUST support the cipher suite with key encapsulation mechanism DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), key derivation function HKDF-SHA256, and authenticated encryption AES-128-GCM.

The client creates a query plaintext, deserializes the target's public key, and computes the encrypted message with encrypt_query_body. That function sets up an HPKE base context with the label "odoh query", uses as associated data the byte 0x01 followed by the length of the key identifier and the key identifier itself, and seals the plaintext. The key identifier is carried outside the encryption so the target can select the right private key.

The target looks up its configuration by the key identifier. If no such key exists it MAY discard the query, and if so it MUST return a 401 Unauthorized response to the proxy. Otherwise it sets up a query context with setup_query_context and decrypts with decrypt_query_body, using the same associated data. If there was no error and the padding is valid, the target resolves the DNS message; otherwise it returns a 400 client error.

For the reply, the target creates a response plaintext and a fresh random nonce of the larger of the nonce and key lengths, then derives the response key and nonce with derive_secrets. That function exports a secret from the HPKE context with the label "odoh response", uses the query plaintext concatenated with the length and value of the nonce as the salt, and expands the result into a key and a nonce. The reply is sealed with associated data of 0x02 followed by the length and value of the nonce, and the nonce is placed in the key_id field so the client can derive the same secrets. The client decrypts with decrypt_response_body and MUST validate that the padding is all zeros before using the DNS message inside.

Because the reply key is derived from the query plaintext, the proxy, which never saw the plaintext, cannot decrypt the answer either.
sections.plainLanguage: The query is sealed with the target's public key, so only the target can open it. The answer is sealed with a key derived from the original question, so the proxy, which only ever saw the ciphertext, cannot open that either. Only the client holds everything needed to read both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Oblivious DoH aims to keep knowledge of the true query origin and its contents known only to clients. The model assumes an extended Dolev-Yao style attacker that can observe all network activity and can adaptively compromise either the proxy or the target, but not the clients. Compromising both is equivalent to collusion between the two parties in practice. Once compromised, the attacker has access to all session information and private key material.

The security properties are stated informally. Queries and answers are known only to clients and targets in possession of the corresponding response key and HPKE keying material. In particular, proxies know the origin and destination of an oblivious query yet do not know the plaintext query, and targets know only the oblivious query origin, that is the proxy, and the plaintext query. Only the client knows both the plaintext query contents and the destination. Target resolvers cannot link queries from the same client in the absence of unique per-client keys.

Traffic analysis mitigations are outside the scope of the document. In particular, it does not prescribe padding lengths for the query and response messages, and implementations SHOULD follow the guidance in RFC 8467 for choosing a padding length. Oblivious DoH security does not depend on proxy and target indistinguishability: an on-path attacker could determine whether a connection to a specific endpoint is used for oblivious or direct queries, but this has no effect on the confidentiality goals.

On denial of service, malicious clients or proxies can send bogus queries to targets, and target servers can throttle processing in response. Since targets give explicit errors upon decryption failure, proxies can throttle specific clients. Targets trust proxies not to overwhelm them, and it is expected that proxies implement some form of rate limiting or client authentication.

Proxies that do not reuse connections to targets for many clients may allow targets to link individual queries to unknown clients, so it is RECOMMENDED that proxies pool and reuse connections to targets, which also benefits performance. Whichever authentication mechanism is in place, proxies MUST NOT reveal any client authentication information to targets, so that targets cannot uniquely identify individual clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The guarantee depends on the proxy and the target not working together. If either one is compromised on its own, the attacker still cannot link a question to the person who asked it. What the scheme does not do is hide that DNS traffic is happening at all, or the timing of the exchanges.

sections.title: Deployment Requirements and the Experiment
sections.content:
Oblivious DoH requires, at a minimum, an Oblivious Proxy server identified by a URI Template, an Oblivious Target server, with the two expected to be non-colluding, and one or more target public keys for encrypting the DNS queries sent to a target via a proxy. These keys guarantee that only the intended target can decrypt client queries. The mechanism for discovering and provisioning the proxy URI Template and the target public keys is out of scope for the document.

Servers ought to rotate public keys regularly, and it is RECOMMENDED that servers rotate keys every day. Shorter rotation windows reduce the anonymity set of clients that might use the public key, while longer rotation windows widen the time frame of possible compromise.

The experiment described in Section 10 is intended to assess deployment configuration viability and related performance impacts on DNS resolution, by measuring key performance indicators such as resolution latency. Participants test various parameters affecting service operation and performance, including mechanisms for discovery and configuration of proxies and targets, as well as the performance implications of connection reuse and pools where appropriate. The results are to influence future protocol design and deployment efforts. Implementations of DoH that are not involved in the experiment will not recognize this protocol and will not take part in it. It is anticipated that the use of Oblivious DoH will be widespread and that the experiment will be of long duration.

For IANA, the document registers a new media type, application/oblivious-dns-message, whose content is an encrypted DNS message and not executable code.
sections.plainLanguage: Running this needs two servers and a way to learn the target's public key. The public key should be changed often, ideally every day, so that a key which leaks is only useful for a short time. The document describes this as an experiment to measure how well it works in practice.

messages.label: POST ENCRYPTED QUERY
messages.note: The query is sealed with the target's public key, so the proxy cannot read it.

messages.label: FORWARD TO TARGET
messages.note: The proxy uses the targethost and targetpath variables from the request URL.

messages.label: ENCRYPTED RESPONSE
messages.note: The answer is sealed with a key derived from the original query.

messages.label: FORWARD RESPONSE
messages.note: The proxy forwards the body and status code without modification.

fields.name: message_type
fields.desc: One byte identifying the message: 0x01 for a query, 0x02 for a response.

fields.name: key_id
fields.desc: Identifier of the target's configuration key in a query; a fresh random nonce in a response.

fields.name: encrypted_message
fields.desc: The encrypted ObliviousDoHMessagePlaintext: the DNS message plus zero padding.

items.title: Client
items.text: Knows the plaintext query and the target it was sent to.

items.title: Proxy
items.text: Knows the client's address and the target, but not the query or the answer.

items.title: Target
items.text: Knows the plaintext query and the proxy that carried it, but not the client's address.
